item.title: My Cosmos World Model Didn’t Know What to Do With a Physics Engine
item.content:encoded:
Cosmos World Model Didn’t Know What to Do With a Physics Engine

Pointing NVIDIA’s Cosmos 3 at a MuJoCo simulator: what failed, what fine-tuning fixed, and what it didn’t

NVIDIA’s Cosmos 3 is an action-conditioned world foundation model. Given a frame and a sequence of robot actions, it predicts the video that follows; Cosmos calls this mode forward dynamics. In principle that makes it a stand-in for a simulator: a policy picks an action, Cosmos predicts what the camera sees next, and no physics engine is needed.

I wanted to use it that way, for pick-and-place, with data from a MuJoCo simulator that renders synthetic scenes. It didn’t work out of the box. Cosmos’s action-conditioning works on real camera footage and barely at all on my renders. Fine-tuning fixes most of that. Then a second limit appears that has nothing to do with the renders.

What kind of world model this is

Cosmos 3 is, first, a video generation model, and even more technically, a world foundation model: given a prompt or an image, it generates video. What makes it a world model for control is action-conditioning: it also takes the actions a robot will perform, and the video it outputs has to be the consequence of those actions. A video generator’s job is a plausible continuation but an action-conditioned model’s job is the continuation that follows from these particular actions, and if we change the actions the video must change.

Cosmos also commits to pixels. It predicts the next frames themselves, as compressed video latents that decode back to images. Not every world model does. Dreamer predicts a compact latent state, the reward and whether the episode ends. JEPA-style models go further and predict only the embedding of the future, on the argument that pixels make the model spend capacity on texture and lighting that don’t matter for deciding what to do.

The pixel route has advantages: we can watch the output and judge it, and the model can learn from any video, with or without actions. The cost is the objective: it rewards convincing video, and convincing video that ignores the actions scores well on it. Both failures in this article are about that objective and what it was learned from.

The first result looked right

The simulator’s actions are 7 numbers; Cosmos’s robot domains expect 10, and a small conversion bridges them. Fed one frame and a real grasp sequence, Cosmos returned a plausible-looking continuation. Before trusting it, I ran a control: the same frame with an all-zero “stay” action. We can measure a prediction’s motion by summing the differences between consecutive frames. The real grasp scored 0.631 and the no-op 0.638. Negating the action’s sign left the motion where it was. Cosmos was generating generic motion and ignoring the numbers.

Scale My actions are in metres and radians. Sweeping a multiplier on them, the motion stayed at the noise floor up to 10× and rose sharply between 20× and 40×. Cosmos’s inverse-dynamics mode, asked what actions it infers from my real footage, reported vertical movements about 12.5× my raw values.

The renderer Scaled into the responsive range, the response on my renders was still weak, the cube moved the wrong way, and at larger multipliers the model hallucinated, which is where the red object in the opening figure comes from. The test that settles it holds the action and scale fixed and swaps only the conditioning image for the real photo that ships with the checkpoint:

On a real image, my converted actions produce a strong response that scales cleanly towards the model’s own ceiling. Swap back to my render with the same action, and it’s weak or hallucinated.

Every one of Cosmos 3’s action-conditioned domains (Bridge, DROID, UMI, Fractal and the rest) was trained on real camera footage. The model has learned how actions move pixels in real video, and it’s unable to apply that to a synthetic frame.

A bigger model fails differently

I was using Cosmos3-Edge, a distilled 4-billion-parameter checkpoint. Cosmos3-Nano has 16 billion and isn’t distilled. It took 30.6 GiB of a 46 GiB GPU to load, and on the same grasp test its motion scores were 0.649 and 0.885 against a no-op of 0.731: the same weak response, with a different failure. Instead of a phantom object, the gripper’s base detached from the arm and floated out of the frame.

The domain gap is a property of what the whole model family was trained on, and size doesn’t close it.

Making the renders look like photographs helps a little

I added a post-processing pass to the simulator: Gaussian blur, sensor noise, vignetting, chromatic aberration and colour jitter, applied after rendering so the physics and recorded actions are untouched. On the clean render, the predicted cube motion pointed the wrong way at every scale; on the processed render it pointed the right way from 18× upward. But the magnitude still undershot the real motion by 2–3×, and at 60× the model hallucinated again. The flat shading is still there under the blur. It isn’t the fix.

Fine-tuning fixes direction, not magnitude

Inside Cosmos 3’s transformer, the only place action tokens can influence the predicted video is a set of attention projections: four modules in each of 28 layers, 112 in all.

That makes the fine-tune, which NVIDIA calls post-training, narrow. I put LoRA, i.e. a small set of extra trainable weights bolted onto a frozen model, on exactly those 112 modules: 3.2 million trainable parameters out of 3.37 billion, or 0.095%. Cosmos also looks up its action-projection weights by domain ID in a table of 32 slots; the shipped domains use 21. I gave my simulator slot 21 and trained its rows from scratch, so the pretrained domains never move and the new slot learns its own action scale from the data.

After an overnight run of 21,483 steps on 800 episodes, the predicted cube moved in the same direction as the real one in 84% of 25 held-out test episodes, up from 60%. The hallucinations are gone.

The ratio of motion between a real action and a no-op was 1.654 before training and 1.644 after. The model has learned which way things go, and it hasn’t learned to move more for a bigger action. Since 26× more steps than the pilot didn’t move that ratio, I read it as a capacity limit of a LoRA this narrow. The next lever is LoRA on the pathway’s MLP blocks as well.

The second wall

To be an environment, a world model has to run on its own output: the policy picks an action, Cosmos predicts the next frame, the policy sees that frame and picks again. The policy here is a ResNet18 trained by behaviour cloning; it succeeds on 86–90% of real-simulator episodes, so it isn’t the weak link.

I ran that loop for 128 steps in two ways.

Anchored: Cosmos predicts each chunk from a real simulator frame, so errors can’t compound.

Pure imagination: Cosmos sees frame 0 and only its own predictions after that.

Anchored tracks the real rollout throughout. Pure imagination holds for about 3 chunks, then the geometry distorts (the arm thins, objects blur into blobs) and, from chunk 4, the lighting washes out.

That comparison has a confound. The policy reacts to what it sees, so once Cosmos drifts it may pick different actions. To isolate the model, I ran a third condition: Cosmos predicting from its own output, driven by the real, correct action sequence throughout, with no policy at all. It drifts just as badly, from about the same chunk, with the same symptoms.

So the instability belongs to Cosmos’s self-conditioning. It shows up after the domain gap is fixed, so it’s a second, separate limit.

The obvious fix didn’t work

The diagnosis points at exposure bias: the model was only ever trained to continue from clean frames, and at inference it has to continue from frames carrying its own artefacts. One possible remedy, called scheduled sampling, is to train on our own imperfect outputs some of the time.

I trained a fresh adapter from the base model with the same recipe and two additions: about 40% of training windows got a perturbed conditioning frame, and periodically the loop rolled the current model forward to generate a conditioning frame and trained the next chunk from it. The run went 18 hours and 34,315 steps on 2,000 episodes.

On three episodes, in both loops, measured as pixel distance from the real frame at each step, the drift was no better than the first adapter’s and slightly worse on most. What that rules out is that a sparse dose of self-conditioning is enough. What’s left is a much higher ratio of self-generated conditioning frames, or more adapter capacity, or both: a narrower problem than the one I started with.

What to expect if you try this

  • If your renderer isn’t photoreal, expect no transfer from a pretrained action-conditioned world model out of the box. A larger checkpoint won’t change that.
  • Budget for fine-tuning, and target it. The action-to-vision pathway here was 0.095% of the parameters, enough to go from hallucination to 84% direction-correctness.
  • Short, re-grounded prediction from a real frame works now. Long autoregressive self-simulation, the thing people mean by “virtual environment”, isn’t there yet for this model on this data.

The code is on GitHub.

NVIDIA, “Cosmos 3: Omnimodal World Models for Physical AI”, arXiv:2606.02800, 2026. Checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge

The simulator and dataset: https://github.com/cydal/mujoco-env-dataset

Hu et al., “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models”, arXiv:2106.09685, 2021.

Bengio et al., “Scheduled Sampling for Sequence Prediction with Recurrent Neural Networks”, NeurIPS 2015.

The Cosmos adapter, validation scripts, fine-tuning and closed-loop code: https://github.com/cydal/cosmos-policy

Elliot Sage., “AI Build & Learn” https://github.com/sagecodes/ai-build-and-learn, 2026

item.title: Every App Switch Is a Doorway. With ADHD, I Forget Why I Walked Through.
item.content:encoded:
There’s real research on why we forget things at doorways. For developers with ADHD, every app switch is one, so I built a Mac file manager with fewer of them.

I opened the terminal to run a script on a CSV file.

Then I realised I didn’t remember the exact filename, so I switched to Finder to check. It was there. I pressed Space to look at it, and Quick Look gave me a wall of commas, so I opened it in another app to see it properly. Something looked off, and I started wondering whether this was the old export, so I opened my FTP client to compare it with the version on the server.

About a minute and a half later I was staring at a folder listing in the FTP client with genuinely no idea what I’d come there to do. The script never ran, and the terminal was still sitting in my home directory where I had left it.

If you have ADHD, I suspect you’ve had some version of that minute. And it turns out there’s a name for what happened.

The doorway effect

Most people have walked into the kitchen and immediately forgotten what they went there for. Psychologists call this the doorway effect, and it has actually been studied. In a series of experiments at the University of Notre Dame (Radvansky & Copeland, 2006; Radvansky, Krawietz & Tamplin, 2011), Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues found that walking through a doorway made people noticeably worse at remembering what they had just been dealing with, compared with walking the same distance within a single room.

The explanation they give, as Radvansky put it in Notre Dame’s write-up of the research, is that our brains chop experience up into episodes, and a doorway works as an event boundary. When you cross one, your mind tidies away the previous scene to make room for the new one, and whatever you were planning to do (get the scissors, find the charger) tends to get tidied away along with it.

What I found most interesting is that the effect also appeared when people walked through doorways in a virtual environment on a computer screen. Nobody left their chair. The doorway only had to feel like a transition from one space to another.

To be clear, those studies were about rooms, not apps, so applying them to software is my own leap. But I recognise the feeling. When I switch from the terminal to Finder, everything changes at once: the window, the layout, the controls, even where my eyes go on the screen. It feels a lot like walking into another room, and on a busy day as a developer I do that hundreds of times.

And then there’s ADHD

I have inattentive ADHD, which mostly means my thoughts drift off quietly and I often don’t notice until I’m somewhere else entirely. But I don’t think you need my particular kind of ADHD for this to land. If you have the hyperactive or combined type, the doorway might trip you up differently: the new window is full of new things, something grabs you, and you’re off doing that instead. Different route, same result. You arrive somewhere and the original plan has gone.

What ADHD in all its forms tends to share is a struggle with working memory, which shows up consistently in research on both children and adults with ADHD. Working memory is the mental scratchpad that keeps track of what am I doing right now, and why. Everyone loses a few notes off that scratchpad at a doorway. With ADHD, mine seems to lose most of them, most of the time.

That’s why, for me, a context switch costs much more than the second it takes to press ⌘-Tab. There’s a real chance that by the time I get to the other side, I’ve already lost the reason I went. Then I either have to rebuild it, or, more often, I get drawn into whatever the new window happens to be showing me.

For years my working day on a Mac was spread across something like this:

  • Terminal to run things
  • Finder to find things
  • A previewer or editor to actually read the Markdown, the CSV, the JSON
  • An FTP, SFTP, or cloud storage client to get to files on a server or in a bucket
  • A git client (or more terminal) to see what had changed

Pretty much every task meant going back and forth between several of those, sometimes many times over, and each of those trips was another doorway.

At some point I accepted that I wasn’t going to get better at doorways, and that it would be more realistic to have fewer of them. That idea eventually turned into Iruka, a native macOS file manager that I build. These days it’s my main workspace. I have it open all day, every day, and I wanted to share it because it has made a real difference to how scattered my days feel. So, with the obvious disclosure that I’m biased, here is how it deals with each of those doorways.

Doorway 1: the terminal (the big one)

This was the doorway that cost me the most.

You find a folder in Finder, switch to Terminal, and then you have to retype the path to the folder you were looking at a second ago, from memory, one cd at a time. Somewhere around cd ~/projects/client- I'd start thinking about the client, then the email I still owed them, and the folder would be forgotten.

In Iruka, the terminal sits underneath the file browser and follows you around. When you browse to a folder, the shell is already there, so there’s no path to retype and no other window to go to.

On paper this sounds like a minor convenience, but for me it’s the difference between going from I want to run this script here straight to running it, versus going from that thought to typing a path and losing the thought halfway.

There are a few details that help me stay on track:

  • It doesn’t get in your way. If something is running, like a build, an editor, a REPL, or an AI agent, Iruka holds back the cd and shows "Sync paused — terminal is busy". Once the command finishes, the terminal catches up to wherever you've browsed in the meantime, so you can keep clicking around while you wait without breaking anything.
  • It also works in the other direction. If you’ve cd'd somewhere in the shell yourself, one button brings the file browser to the terminal's folder. It doesn't matter which side you wandered off with, the other one can catch up.
  • You can stay on the keyboard. ⌘⌥T switches focus between the browser and the terminal, and F4 hides the terminal without stopping whatever is running in it.

This became even more useful once AI coding agents started living in the terminal. I browse to a folder, type claude, and the agent starts in exactly the folder I'm looking at. I've written about that workflow separately.

Doorway 2: “let me just open that in something that can read it”

A lot of what’s on my disk is text: Markdown notes, CSV exports, JSON, HTML reports, source code. Finder’s Quick Look shows most of it as raw text, full of asterisks, pound signs and commas.

So I used to spot a file, open it in a separate app to read it properly, and by the time that app had started up and arranged its windows, I’d walked through another doorway.

Iruka renders these files right next to the file list:

  • Markdown as a properly formatted document, with headings, tables and code blocks
  • CSV as a scrollable grid with a header row
  • Code with syntax highlighting for over 60 languages
  • HTML as the rendered page (scripts don’t run and nothing is loaded from the network, so it’s a safe way to look at a generated report)

When I notice something wrong, like a typo in a config file or a value that’s off, there’s an Edit button right in the preview. I fix it, it saves automatically, and I carry on, without launching an editor or finding the same file again.

This one matters to me more than it might seem. With ADHD, small problems that I notice but can’t fix immediately have a habit of never getting fixed at all. If fixing something means opening another app, there’s a good chance I won’t come back to it. If it’s one click away, it actually gets done.

Doorway 3: the FTP or cloud client

This was the doorway that took me furthest away from what I was doing. A server is a different machine, so it always seemed natural that it would live in a different app.

But a different app means getting used to a different layout and different shortcuts every time you switch, and on top of that I’d usually need a separate SSH window, where I’d navigate to the same remote folder all over again just to run a command there.

In Iruka, remote storage shows up as ordinary folders:

  • sFTP: you save a server once, right-click it and choose Mount as SFTP, and then you browse it like any local folder.
  • FTP and S3-compatible cloud storage (Amazon S3, Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, MinIO) are mounted in the same way.
  • SMB, AFP, NFS and WebDAV are mounted natively through macOS.

The bit I’m proudest of is that when you browse an SFTP mount, the SSH terminal follows you on the server. If you browse into /home/demo/results, the shell underneath is in /home/demo/results on the remote machine. It feels like the server is just another folder in the same room.

If you put your Mac on one side and the server on the other in dual pane mode, and turn on View → Show Both Terminals, you can run something on the server, look at the output, drag it over to your Mac, and run a local command on the copy, all without leaving the window. (SFTP, FTP and cloud mounts need a one-time setup, which I go through in the SFTP walkthrough.)

Doorway 4: carrying things from room to room

This one feels very ADHD to me. Say I need three files from three different folders copied into one place. The usual way is to copy one, go to the destination, paste it, go back, find the next one, and so on. Every time I go back, I risk forgetting which file I needed next, or getting distracted by something else in that folder.

Iruka has a Drop Stack, a little shelf at the top of the sidebar. As you come across files you need, you drag them onto it. It doesn’t copy anything at that point; it just remembers where they are. When you get to the destination, you click Copy Here or Move Here.

For me it works a bit like a notepad for working memory: the shelf keeps track of what I’m carrying, so I don’t have to hold it in my head. It’s shared across tabs and windows, it’s still there after you quit the app, and both actions can be undone with ⌘Z if you click the wrong thing.

Doorway 5: finding your way back after you drift off anyway

None of this makes me impossible to distract. I still drift off, a notification still gets me sometimes, and I still come back to a folder twenty minutes later wondering what on earth I was doing there.

A couple of things help me pick up where I left off:

  • The file list shows what changed. In a git repository, changed files get a small status badge right in the list, so you can see what you (or your AI agent) were working on before you got sidetracked.
  • The Review pane shows exactly how they changed. It lists every changed file, with a line-by-line diff, right next to the browser. It’s the closest thing I have to a note from my past self saying where I was.

If I can’t remember where something was, I can type a path in the URL bar with Tab autocomplete, the same way I would in a shell. Or I can use Power Search, which searches file contents with grep and regex and doesn’t need an index, so “it had the word ‘threshold’ in it somewhere” is enough to find a file.

What this is, and what it isn’t

I want to be careful here, because there’s a lot of overpromising around ADHD.

A file manager isn’t a treatment. It won’t fix your attention or make you finish things. What it can do is cut down on how often your tools force you to rebuild your train of thought from scratch. For me, having fewer doorways means losing the thread less often, and when I do lose it, I get back on track more quickly. That holds whichever way your ADHD shows up, and probably even if you don’t have ADHD at all.

Iruka also isn’t an IDE. There’s no debugger or language server, and the editing in the preview pane is meant for quick fixes. It’s first and foremost a Finder replacement, with dual panes, tabs, batch rename and list/column/icon views, written natively in Swift and quick to start. Removing doorways is simply how it turned out, because I was building it for my own head, and it’s now where I spend most of my working day.

If any of this sounds like your day, try it on a real task rather than a demo. Pick something that usually has you bouncing between three apps, and see how many doorways are left.

brew install --cask dorienh/iruka/iruka

You can also download it from iruka.sh. It runs on macOS 14 or later, on both Apple Silicon and Intel.

And if you have ADHD, whichever kind, and you run into a doorway I haven’t dealt with yet, please tell me on GitHub Discussions. I read every post, several features have come straight from there, and I’d love the next one to come from someone whose brain works a bit like mine.

Dorien Herremans is as associate professor at Singapore University of Technology and Design. She is also the developer of Iruka and has inattentive ADHD. This article is based on personal experience and isn’t medical advice.

References

  • Radvansky, G. A., & Copeland, D. E. (2006). Walking through doorways causes forgetting: Situation models and experienced space. Memory & Cognition, 34(5), 1150–1156.
  • Radvansky, G. A., Krawietz, S. A., & Tamplin, A. K. (2011). Walking through doorways causes forgetting: Further explorations. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(8), 1632–1645.
  • University of Notre Dame (2011). Walking through doorways causes forgetting, new research shows.
  • Kasper, L. J., Alderson, R. M., & Hudec, K. L. (2012). Moderators of working memory deficits in children with ADHD: A meta-analytic review. Clinical Psychology Review, 32(7), 605–617.
  • Alderson, R. M., Kasper, L. J., Hudec, K. L., & Patros, C. H. G. (2013). Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and working memory in adults: A meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology, 27(3), 287–302.

item.title: TanStack Router Does Something React Router Still Can’t.
item.content:encoded:
TanStack Router Does Something React Router Still Can’t. Most React Developers Haven’t Switched Yet.

React Router has 53 million weekly downloads. TanStack Router has 8 million. The gap isn’t because React Router is better it’s because most teams haven’t realized what they’re giving up by staying.

Here’s a bug you’ve probably shipped.

A page in your React app expects a URL like `/users?sort=createdAt&page=2`. Someone navigates to `/users?sort=CREATEDAT&page=two`. Your component crashes, or silently renders with a wrong state, because the search params you got back from `useSearchParams()` are strings and React Router trusts you to validate them yourself.

You didn’t. Nobody does. The types said `string`. You assumed the URL would be valid.

With TanStack Router, this class of bug doesn’t exist. Search params are defined with a schema, validated at the routing layer, and returned as typed values. If the URL has `page=two`, TanStack Router catches it before your component ever runs. The type isn’t `string` it’s `number`, because you said it was `number`, and the router enforces it.

That’s the core of what TanStack Router does differently. And it goes further than search params.

The problem React Router has always had

React Router is string-based routing. Every param that comes out of `useParams()` is a string. Every search param from `useSearchParams()` is a string. You cast them yourself:

// React Router - you handle the casting
const { userId } = useParams();
const id = parseInt(userId!, 10); // What if it's undefined? What if it's "abc"?
const [searchParams] = useSearchParams();
const page = parseInt(searchParams.get("page") ?? "1", 10); // Hope for the best
const sort = searchParams.get("sort") as "createdAt" | "name"; // This is lying to TypeScript

TypeScript sees `userId` as `string | undefined`. It sees `page` as `number` after your cast but TypeScript believed you when you cast, even if the actual value is `NaN`. The type system and the runtime have silently parted ways.

React Router v7 (which merged with Remix) improved this in framework mode with a codegen step if you use the full framework setup, you get typed `loaderData` and route params. But search params remain manual string handling even there.

What TanStack Router actually does differently

TanStack Router is built from the ground up with TypeScript. The route tree itself is a type. Every piece of navigation data path params, search params, loader return values is inferred from how you define the route.

Type-safe path params no casting needed:

// TanStack Router - params are inferred from the route definition
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';
export const Route = createFileRoute('/users/$userId')({
 component: UserPage,
});
function UserPage() {
 const { userId } = Route.useParams();
 // userId is string - but TypeScript knows it MUST exist
 // No "string | undefined". No non-null assertions.
}

Type-safe search params validated at the routing layer:

import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import { z } from 'zod';
const searchSchema = z.object({
 page: z.number().int().positive().default(1),
 sort: z.enum(['createdAt', 'name', 'email']).default('createdAt'),
 query: z.string().optional(),
});
export const Route = createFileRoute('/users')({
 validateSearch: searchSchema,
 component: UsersPage,
});
function UsersPage() {
 const { page, sort, query } = Route.useSearch();
 // page is number - not string, not string | undefined, not a cast
 // sort is 'createdAt' | 'name' | 'email' - TypeScript knows the valid values
 // If the URL has ?page=two, the router applies the default before your component runs
}

The difference isn’t syntactic. The type system and the runtime are describing the same thing. A `page` that TypeScript says is `number` is actually a `number` at runtime, because the router validated it before handing it to the component.

Type-safe navigation the part that catches bugs before they happen

This is where the gap becomes most visible in day-to-day development.

With React Router, a `<Link>` is a string:

// React Router - nothing checks this
<Link to="/users/abc?sort=WRONG&page=two">View Users</Link>
// Typo in path? Compiles fine.
// Wrong sort value? Compiles fine.
// page as string instead of number? Compiles fine.

With TanStack Router, `<Link>` is typed:

// TanStack Router - TypeScript checks everything
<Link
 to="/users"
 search={{ sort: 'createdAt', page: 1 }}
>
 View Users
</Link>
// Change a route's params?
// TypeScript finds every broken Link in your codebase immediately.
// Before you run the app. Before you deploy.

If you rename a route or change which params it accepts, TypeScript surfaces every navigation that breaks across your entire codebase, at compile time. This is the feature that React Router teams feel most acutely when they switch: they stop discovering broken navigation in QA.

Loader data typed all the way through

TanStack Router’s loaders are type-safe too. The return type of your loader flows directly into `Route.useLoaderData()` with no manual annotation:

export const Route = createFileRoute('/users/$userId')({
 loader: async ({ params }) => {
 // params.userId is string - typed from the route definition
 const user = await fetchUser(params.userId);
 return { user }; // TypeScript infers { user: User }
 },
 component: UserPage,
});
function UserPage() {
 const { user } = Route.useLoaderData();
 // user is User - inferred from the loader return type
 // No manual annotation. No "as User" cast.
}

This matters most on large teams where the person writing the component isn’t always the person who wrote the loader. The types document the contract between them, automatically.

The file-based routing setup

TanStack Router defaults to file-based routing, where your route tree is generated automatically from your file structure. The `@tanstack/router-plugin` watches your `routes/` directory and generates a typed route tree that powers all the type inference above.

src/routes/
 __root.tsx → the root layout
 index.tsx → /
 users/
 index.tsx → /users
 $userId.tsx → /users/:userId
 $userId/
 posts.tsx → /users/:userId/posts

The generated `routeTree.gen.ts` file is what TypeScript uses to know that `/users/$userId` requires a `userId` param, that the `/users` route accepts `page` and `sort` search params, and that navigating to a path that doesn’t exist in the tree is a type error.

You never edit the generated file the plugin handles it. You get the type safety for free.

How it compares to React Router v7 in framework mode

React Router v7 (framework mode) closes some of the gap through a similar codegen approach. The `Route` types it generates give you typed `loaderData` and typed path params. This is a real improvement over React Router v6.

The places where TanStack Router still wins:

Search params. React Router v7 framework mode still treats search params as strings inside loaders. TanStack Router validates and types them at the schema level.

Link type safety. React Router’s `<Link>` component accepts any string. TanStack Router’s `<Link>` is typed to the route tree.

SPA mode. TanStack Router is designed for client-side SPAs. React Router v7 framework mode is designed for SSR if you’re building a Vite SPA (not a full-stack app), TanStack Router is a more natural fit.

TanStack ecosystem integration. TanStack Router integrates natively with TanStack Query. Search params can drive queries. Loader data flows into components. The whole data layer speaks the same type language.

Where React Router v7 still wins: SSR, mature documentation, ecosystem size (53M vs 8M weekly downloads), and Remix migration path. If you’re building something that needs server-side rendering and you want the Remix mental model, React Router v7 is the correct choice.

The actual migration cost

Migrating an existing React Router codebase to TanStack Router is a meaningful project. The mental model is different enough that a large codebase requires a deliberate rewrite of the routing layer, not just a find-and-replace.

The honest assessment:

- New projects: TanStack Router is the clear choice for TypeScript-heavy SPAs, dashboards, and internal tools. Start here.
- Existing projects (small-medium): Worth evaluating. The type safety payoff is real enough that teams report finding bugs they didn’t know they had during migration.
- Existing projects (large, mature): The migration cost is high. Unless your team is feeling the pain of routing-related bugs regularly, staying on React Router v7 is often the right call — the ecosystem and documentation are more established.

The key question: how often do routing bugs show up in your QA or production? If the answer is “regularly” wrong params, broken navigation after a rename, search state drift TanStack Router’s compile-time guarantees address exactly those failure modes.

The thing nobody mentions about adoption

TanStack Router has 8.5 million weekly downloads. React Router has 53 million. That gap is not because React Router is better it’s because most teams haven’t had a forcing function to switch.

The teams that switched are concentrated in a specific category: TypeScript-heavy SPAs, dashboards, B2B tools, admin panels applications where routing complexity is high and type safety actually matters. In those categories, TanStack Router’s adoption is accelerating. TanStack Start (the full-stack framework built on TanStack Router) is pulling more teams in from the full-stack side.

The question isn’t whether TanStack Router will continue growing. It will. The question is whether the gap between “React Router teams” and “TanStack Router teams” closes gradually or suddenly and the answer depends on how many teams hit the same runtime routing bugs that make the type safety argument obvious.

Starting a new project today

For a new Vite + React SPA in 2026, the setup is straightforward:

npm install @tanstack/react-router @tanstack/router-plugin
// vite.config.ts
import { TanStackRouterVite } from '@tanstack/router-plugin/vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
export default defineConfig({
 plugins: [
 TanStackRouterVite(), // generates routeTree.gen.ts automatically
 react(),
 ],
});
// src/main.tsx
import { RouterProvider, createRouter } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import { routeTree } from './routeTree.gen'; // auto-generated
const router = createRouter({ routeTree });
// TypeScript now knows your entire route tree
declare module '@tanstack/react-router' {
 interface Register {
 router: typeof router;
 }
}

From here, every route file you create in `src/routes/` is automatically typed. Every `<Link>`, every `useParams()`, every `useSearch()` reflects the route tree TypeScript has analyzed.

The bugs you were shipping with string-based routing stop shipping. Not because you wrote more validation code because the router validates for you, at compile time.

TanStack Router Does Something React Router Still Can’t. was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
